Most of the newspaper coverage of the just-released Census Bureau data on health insurance coverage has focused changes in coverage between 2009 and 2010. Since the advent of the Great Recession, the reduction in health insurance coverage has been dominated by the simple fact that as unemployment has risen, since most families with prime-age earners receive health insurance as a fringe benefit of employment, the number of uninsured has risen. The increase was large from 2008 to 2009 when unemployment rose rapidly. From 2009 to 2010, when unemployment stabilized at high levels, the increase was smaller, although still disturbingly large.
If one looks back a bit farther, however, some noteworthy differences by age group emerge, as shown in the table at the end of this post. Health insurance coverage fell for all age groups but one from 2007 to 2010 and over the longer period starting with the boom year of 1999. That coverage would have fallen in both periods is unsurprising because, as noted, health insurance for most people is linked to employment and unemployment rose over both of those periods.
The age group that stands as the major exception to this record of declining coverage is children through age 18. That coverage for this group rose over both of those periods is striking. Furthermore, although coverage of the elderly fell, the drop was minuscule. What is going on?
The answer is that the safety net is working. The proportion of young people insured privately declined as much as did that of older age groups, but total coverage of this age group not only was sustained but actually increased. The State Child Health Insurance program, enacted in 1997, has dramatically increased coverage for youngsters. Medicaid expansions mostly enacted earlier have helped expand coverage among the young as their parents have lost coverage through work.
In combination, the number of children age 18 or younger with Medicaid coverage rose by 11.3 million since 1999 and by 5.1 million since 2007. Without this expansion (and assuming no other offsets), the number of uninsured Americans would have been not 49.9 million, but more than 60 million.
These developments take on particular salience in light of the current debate about how best to control federal budget deficits. If Congress, in the end, adheres to the principle, embodied in the August 2010 debt-ceiling legislation, that programs protecting the poor should be insulated from budget cuts, the gains in coverage among the young may be sustained, despite the erosion of employment-based coverage that has been going on for more than a decade. If it abandons this principle, the increase in 'health-insecurity' would be large and deeply troubling.

Question: Did the number of uninsured people increase from 2009 to 2010? Answer: Yes, but at a smaller rate than from 2008 to 2009.

Question: Which age group had an increase in health insurance coverage from 2007 to 2010? Answer: Children through age 18.

Issue: The United States has made historic progress on insurance coverage since the Affordable Care Act became law in 2010, with 20 million fewer people uninsured. Who Is Underinsured?

In this analysis, we use a measure of underinsurance that takes into account an insured adult's reported out-of-pocket costs over the course of a year, not including premiums, and his or her health plan deductible. out-of-pocket costs, excluding premiums, over the prior 12 months are equal to 10 percent or more of household income; or

deductible is 5 percent or more of household income.

The out-of-pocket cost component of the measure is only triggered if a person uses his or her plan. The Affordable Care Act (ACA) has transformed the health insurance market, allowing Americans who lack job-based health benefits access to affordable health insurance options. The law's coverage expansions and protections have reduced the number of uninsured adults by more than 20 million.

content.text:
“Health care as a right” is best understood as a commitment that government guarantee access to a defined package of medically necessary services and protect people from unaffordable costs, rather than leave access primarily to ability to pay. [shard_06052_28767]

That principle does not by itself specify single-payer insurance, government-owned hospitals, free care at the point of service, or any other particular institutional design. [shard_06052_28767]

Universal coverage has at least three separate dimensions: who is covered, which services are covered, and how much of the cost the public system pays. [shard_06052_28767]

A serious endorsement should therefore ask the campaign to define its promised benefit package, eligibility rules, cost-sharing protections, financing, provider-payment policy, and implementation timetable rather than treating the slogan as a complete policy. [shard_06052_28767]

Coverage is necessary for equity but does not equal affordability, because people can possess insurance while facing deductibles, premiums, excluded services, or copayments that deter care. [shard_06253_9071]

In one national survey, 28 percent of continuously insured working-age adults were underinsured in 2016, and 52 percent of underinsured adults reported medical-bill or medical-debt problems. [shard_06253_9071]

More recent evidence on adults aged 50 to 64 with employer coverage likewise found that low-income enrollees frequently struggled with premiums, skipped care because of cost, and carried medical debt despite being insured. [shard_00080_80914]

The board should treat reductions in medical debt and delayed care as explicit success measures, not assume that extending an insurance card will achieve them. [shard_05463_23558] [shard_00080_80914]

Medical debt can constrain employment, family decisions, credit, and access to future opportunity, which gives the “right” framing a concrete financial-protection rationale beyond expanding enrollment. [shard_05463_23558]

Medicaid expansion is a comparatively incremental route toward that goal because it extends eligibility to almost all adults below a specified income threshold and uses enhanced federal financing, while also covering people with substantial behavioral-health needs. [shard_02259_81846]

Evidence reviewed here associates Medicaid expansion with better access to behavioral-health services, less unmet need, improved coordination, and lower uncompensated-care costs for providers. [shard_02259_81846]

Its weaknesses are dependence on federal-state cooperation, uneven state participation, administrative eligibility rules, low provider payment in some settings, and exposure to proposals for work requirements, enrollment caps, block grants, or per-person funding limits. [shard_02259_81846]

Those design choices matter because capped funding can shift fiscal risk to states and create pressure to reduce eligibility, benefits, provider payments, or services when economic conditions or health crises increase demand. [shard_02259_81846]

Employer-based insurance offers group purchasing, employer contributions, broad networks, and administrative convenience, but it ties coverage to employment, can restrict plan and provider choice, and can impose job lock and coverage gaps during unemployment or job changes. [shard_00091_70033] [shard_04309_57791]

Employment-linked coverage also makes the system vulnerable to recessions, since loss of work can mean loss of insurance, although Medicaid and children’s coverage have historically buffered some of that erosion. [shard_04309_57791]

A rights-based policy could preserve employer plans while guaranteeing a public fallback, or replace them with a common financing system; the crucial test is whether changing jobs, becoming sick, or having low income changes one’s entitlement to care. [shard_00091_70033] [shard_06052_28767]

Emergency departments and community safety-net clinics would remain essential even under broad coverage because they serve people with unstable coverage, complex needs, behavioral-health problems, and limited access to primary or specialty care. [shard_05932_11825] [shard_02259_81846]

Universal coverage should not be sold as an automatic reduction in emergency-room use, because an Oregon Medicaid study found that newly insured adults used emergency departments about 40 percent more, including for conditions treatable in primary care, at an estimated additional cost of $120 per person annually. [shard_02772_52926]

The practical implication is to finance primary care, behavioral health, transportation, care coordination, rural capacity, and safety-net workforce development alongside coverage expansion rather than expecting insurance alone to redirect patients. [shard_05932_11825] [shard_02772_52926]

Single-payer would make government the principal payer and could broaden access, negotiate prices, and reduce the duplication associated with multiple insurers, but it would require substantial public revenue and could produce disputes over taxes, provider payment, treatment limits, waiting times, and private supplemental coverage. [shard_02199_59748]

The tax question should be framed as a distributional comparison, not simply as “higher taxes versus no cost,” because the current system already combines public spending, employer contributions, worker premiums, deductibles, tax subsidies, and medical bills. [shard_02206_56548]

The United States spends heavily while incurring high prices and substantial administrative costs, and the tax exclusion for employer-paid premiums represents a large public subsidy that is less targeted by income than many explicit assistance programs. [shard_02206_56548]

A fiscally credible proposal should show its gross public cost, offsetting reductions in employer premiums and household out-of-pocket spending, effects on state budgets, revenue sources, transition costs, and sensitivity to higher-than-expected utilization. [shard_02206_56548] [shard_02772_52926]

Patient choice is a genuine tradeoff: a common public plan can provide portability and equalize access, while narrower provider payment or network rules may limit clinicians, hospitals, treatments, or private-plan alternatives. [shard_02199_59748] [shard_02672_51342]

Implementation risk is particularly serious where reform changes payment rates, because hospitals and physicians may reduce participation or face financial stress if public reimbursement is substantially below current commercial rates. [shard_02672_51342]

Equity also requires more than universal enrollment, since racial and ethnic disparities can persist after insurance coverage is equalized because of language, transportation, geography, provider availability, and differences in quality of care. [shard_05998_7684]

For a statewide nonprofit, the most defensible position may be to endorse the right-to-care principle conditionally while demanding a policy platform that guarantees universal enrollment, income-sensitive cost sharing, protection from medical debt, continuous coverage across employment transitions, adequate provider payments, investment in safety-net capacity, transparent financing, and measurable equity outcomes. [shard_06052_28767] [shard_00080_80914] [shard_05932_11825]

That position supports equity without pretending that the slogan resolves the central fiscal and operational questions, and it leaves the board free to support Medicaid expansion, a public option, regulated multipayer coverage, or single-payer only after comparing their concrete benefits, taxes, risks, and implementation safeguards. [shard_02259_81846] [shard_02199_59748]
